title: Bo: tell your child (Exodus 13:8)
hook: "thou shalt tell thy son in that day", the root of the seder's telling
tomorrow: Bo: a sign upon your hand (Exodus 13:9, 16)

segments.voice: Yesterday a people still in Egypt was handed its own calendar. Your line was own your time. Today, the last night in Egypt turns into a story.

Some families have one story that gets told at every holiday. The time the car broke down in the snow. How Grandma crossed the border with one suitcase. The kids roll their eyes, and then one year a kid tells it themselves, gets the details slightly wrong, someone corrects them, and that's how you know it's alive. The Torah sees this coming. Before the Israelites have even left Egypt, before the sea, before Sinai, it's already planning how the story will be told to children who weren't there.
screen: `THE STORY TOLD EVERY HOLIDAY.` → `ONE YEAR, A KID TELLS IT.` → `PLANNED BEFORE THE EXODUS.`

segments.voice: The verse, in the old Jewish translation, begins: "And thou shalt tell thy son in that day." The Hebrew for and thou shalt tell is v'higadta, from the verb l'haggid, to tell. From that verb comes today's word: haggadah, the telling. It's the name of the little book on the table at the Passover seder, the script for retelling the Exodus, with questions, songs, and food you eat for the story's sake. The Torah talks about children asking about the Exodus in four places, and the rabbis noticed each one sounds different. So the Haggadah sets four children around the table: one wise, one wicked, one simple, and one who doesn't know how to ask. This verse belongs to that fourth child. Nobody asks a question here. The parent just begins. For the one who can't ask, the Haggadah says, in effect, you open the story. Then look at the rest of the verse. The parent says the LORD did this for me, when I came out of Egypt. For me, not for our ancestors. The Mishnah turns that into a rule: in every generation, a person should see themselves as if they personally came out of Egypt. That's why the Haggadah is a telling, not a history lesson. Each generation tells it as its own story, so the next one can.
screen: `V'HIGADTA: AND THOU SHALT TELL.` · `HAGGADAH: THE TELLING.` · `FOUR CHILDREN, ONE WHO CAN'T ASK.` · `FOR ME, AS IF I CAME OUT.` · then, large: `TELL YOUR CHILD.`

segments.voice: Think of one story from your family or your own life that a younger person should know: how someone arrived, how something was survived, a kindness that changed things. Let it play through once the way you'd actually say it out loud, and notice where you'd say we and where you'd say I. If no children are in your life, think of a niece, a student, a younger friend.
Haggadah. The telling. From the verb in thou shalt tell thy son, and the name of the book read at the Passover seder.
Your line: tell your child. Year two so far: the scroll rolling on, come, not go, the darkness, the moon, and now the telling. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: At the Passover seder, Jewish families read the Haggadah together: children ask four questions, the Exodus is retold with food, songs and four cups of wine, and the passage of the four children is read aloud.
